Tbilisi

Georgia's capital in a narrow valley on the Mtkvari — old town, sulphur baths and the starting point of almost every route.

Click a marker for details. Coloured lines are ready-made road trips.

Tbilisi sits on both banks of the Mtkvari in a narrow valley, hemmed in by wooded ridges, and that shape explains most of the city. The historic centre is small enough to walk: Narikala Fortress on the ridge above, the brick domes of the Abanotubani sulphur baths in the gorge below, and within a few hundred metres of one another a mosque, a synagogue and an Armenian church.

A second day opens the city up. The Mtatsminda funicular climbs to a park and a terrace high above the rooftops. The Georgian National Museum on Rustaveli holds the gold of the Colchian burials and the permanent exhibition on the Soviet occupation. Holy Trinity Cathedral, huge and modern, stands over Avlabari on the opposite bank. On the green edge of town, Turtle Lake sits beside the Open Air Museum of Ethnography, where timber houses brought from every province are reassembled among the trees, and further north the columns of the Chronicle of Georgia rise above the Tbilisi Sea.

Seasons matter less here than anywhere else in the country, since everything is open year-round. July and August are heavy — the valley traps heat and the afternoons drag — so sightseeing works best early and late in the day. Spring and autumn are the good months. Winter is mild and snow rarely lasts more than a day or two.

Two days cover the centre comfortably, three if you want a bathhouse, a museum and an unhurried evening. Most visitors also treat Tbilisi as a base: Mtskheta is half an hour out, Gori a little over an hour, Kakheti under two. It is both a destination and the place where a Georgian road trip begins and ends.

Best for

  • Two days of city walking before heading out
  • A base for day trips to Mtskheta, Gori and Kakheti
  • Sulphur baths, carved balconies and wine bars
  • Collecting or returning a rental car

Driving conditions

Driving in Tbilisi is the least enjoyable part of a Georgian trip. Traffic is dense, lane discipline is loose, minibuses stop wherever a passenger waves, and cars change lanes with little warning. None of it is dangerous at city speeds, but it rewards patience rather than assertion. The urban limit is 50 km/h, speed cameras are common on the main avenues, and the rush hours run roughly 08:30–10:00 and 17:30–19:30.

Parking is the real problem. Street parking in the central districts is zonal and paid, enforced by patrol cameras, and around Abanotubani and the Old Town there is effectively none. Use a paid lot or a shopping-centre garage and walk in. The old lanes are narrow, steep and frequently one-way, so a large car becomes a liability. An economy model handles the city and the highways out of it; see the fleet if the mountains come later.
